title: The festival after Ramadan (Eid al-Fitr)
description: What Eid prayer is, what the morning looks like, and how to handle Eid when you are new or on your own.
intro: Eid al-Fitr is the celebration at the end of Ramadan. Keep your first one simple: check the local prayer time, turn up clean and modestly dressed, greet people, and ask your masjid about Zakat al-Fitr in case it applies to you.
summary: Eid prayer is usually early in the morning and much busier than an ordinary prayer.
Wear clean, tidy clothes you can pray in. Cultural clothing is optional.
Eid Mubarak is the greeting if you want an easy one.
Ask your masjid how they collect Zakat al-Fitr, and ask before the prayer.
focusNow: Confirm the Eid date, the prayer time, and the location with a local masjid.
Sort out how you are getting there, where you will park, and what happens to your shoes.
Have one person or group in mind to greet so you are not standing on your own the whole time.
If you are unsure about Zakat al-Fitr, ask early.
canWait: Hosting a big Eid meal.
Buying cultural clothing you cannot afford.
Learning every Eid custom in every Muslim culture.
Detailed rulings on missed fasts, until you can ask a qualified teacher.

sections.heading: What Eid prayer is
sections.body: Eid prayer is a congregational prayer held once Ramadan has ended. It happens in a masjid, a rented hall, a park, or whatever large space the community can get. The details differ locally, so follow what your masjid tells you.

sections.heading: Before you go
items: Check the date the night before. Local moon-sighting announcements do not always agree.
Find the address of the prayer itself, which is often not the usual masjid. Some communities rent a bigger hall for the morning.
Get there early, especially if parking is tight.
Bring a small bag for your shoes if the place will be packed.
Eat something small before you leave, since this is the Eid where the fasting has ended.

sections.heading: What to wear
sections.body: Wear clean, modest clothes you can pray in comfortably. You do not need an Arab, South Asian, Turkish, African, or any other cultural outfit for Eid. Dress up if you enjoy that. Keep it simple if you do not.

sections.heading: What to expect
items: The prayer is short. The crowd is not.
There is usually a khutbah or a short reminder afterwards.
People greet each other, hug, take photos, and often head out for breakfast.
If the crowd gets to be too much, you can go home after the prayer.

sections.heading: If you are on your own
sections.body: Eid can ache when your family is not Muslim or you have not made close Muslim friends yet. Make one concrete plan: go to the prayer, message a mentor, join a community breakfast, or ask one person for coffee. A small Eid is still Eid.

sections.heading: Zakat al-Fitr in brief
sections.body: Many Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr before the Eid prayer as a charity tied to Ramadan. The amount, who has to pay it, and how it gets collected all depend on local scholarly guidance. Ask your masjid early rather than working it out in the parking lot.

sections.heading: After Eid: six days of Shawwal
sections.body: Eid day itself is not a day for fasting. After it, many Muslims fast six days of Shawwal, the month that follows Ramadan. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that fasting Ramadan and then six days of Shawwal is like fasting perpetually (Sahih Muslim 1164). If you owe make-up days, ask a teacher which to do first.

scripts.title: Asking a masjid
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm a new Muslim getting ready for my first Eid. Could you tell me the Eid prayer time, where it's being held, and how the masjid handles Zakat al-Fitr?

scripts.title: At work or school
scripts.body: Eid is a major religious holiday for me. I'd like to ask for the morning off for the prayer and to spend some time with family and community.

scripts.title: With non-Muslim family
scripts.body: Eid is the celebration at the end of Ramadan. I'll be at a morning prayer, and I'd still like to see you later in the day if that works for you.

relatedLinks.label: Eid greetings and other everyday phrases

title: Pilgrimage season (Dhul Hijjah, Hajj and Umrah)
description: The first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, Eid al-Adha, and the basics of pilgrimage, without the advanced rulings.
intro: Dhul Hijjah holds the days of Hajj and Eid al-Adha. Most new Muslims are not going to Hajj this year, and you can still get a lot out of the season through prayer, fasting if you are able, charity, remembrance, and learning how the whole thing fits together.
summary: The first ten days are a time for extra worship and good deeds.
Fasting on the Day of Arafah is recommended for anyone not on Hajj who is able to fast.
Hajj becomes an obligation once a Muslim is physically and financially able to go.
Umrah is a separate pilgrimage you can make outside the Hajj season, though the travel rules still need checking against official sources.
focusNow: Learn what Dhul Hijjah is and mark the first ten days in your calendar.
Pick one or two extra acts: dhikr, charity, Quran, fasting, or being better to your family.
Ask your masjid how Eid al-Adha prayer and qurbani or udhiyah work locally.
If you are planning Hajj or Umrah, check the current Government of Canada travel advisory and the official platforms before you pay anyone.
canWait: The detailed rulings on Hajj rites, if you are not traveling soon.
Comparing every qurbani organization.
Buying a travel package before you have checked the official requirements.
Feeling guilty about not fasting every one of the ten days.

sections.heading: The first ten days
sections.body: The first ten days of Dhul Hijjah are treated as a season for worship. A beginner can keep it practical: more dhikr, a little Quran, some charity, one relationship repaired, and a few days of fasting if your health and schedule allow.

sections.heading: A note on fasting Arafah
sections.body: For Muslims who are not on Hajj, fasting the Day of Arafah is strongly encouraged in hadith. If fasting is medically risky, unsafe for you, or unclear because of your circumstances, ask someone qualified and do a different good deed instead.

sections.heading: Eid al-Adha basics
sections.body: Eid al-Adha falls during the Hajj season and goes back to the story of Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Communities hold an Eid prayer, and many Muslims arrange qurbani or udhiyah through organizations they trust.

sections.heading: Qurbani and udhiyah in brief
sections.body: Qurbani, also called udhiyah, is the sacrifice offered around Eid al-Adha by those it applies to. The details shift depending on school of law, income, what is available locally, and which charity you use. Ask your local imam or a trusted organization instead of treating a checkout page as a ruling.

sections.heading: Hajj as something ahead of you
sections.body: Hajj is one of the pillars of Islam for those who are able to go. New Muslims usually need time first: steady prayer, money, travel documents, family responsibilities, health. Understanding the shape of it is enough for now unless you are actively booking travel.

sections.heading: Umrah basics
sections.body: Umrah is a pilgrimage to Makkah outside the Hajj season. It is worship, and it is also visas, health, money, safety, and careful travel planning. Use the official platforms and current government guidance before you book.

sections.heading: Getting ready in body and paperwork
items: The Government of Canada travel page expects the next Hajj around 14 to 19 May 2027. It warns that heat in Saudi Arabia goes well above 40 degrees Celsius, that dehydration and heatstroke can be fatal, and that the crowds bring a risk of crushes.
Start walking regularly months before you go. Hajj and Umrah involve a lot of walking, often in heat.

Book a travel clinic visit well ahead. The official Hajj health rules are on Nusuk, and the clinic can check which vaccines apply to you. The travel.gc.ca page says proof of yellow fever vaccination is needed only if you arrive from, or pass through, a country with yellow fever.
Ask your masjid for a certificate of your conversion early. It can be needed for Hajj or Umrah applications, and it takes time to arrange.

Read the travel advisory again before you pay anyone. If a package looks like a scam, report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, whose vacation fraud page describes fake cheap trips and requests for deposits.

sections.heading: Checking the official route
items: Check the current Government of Canada travel advisory for Saudi Arabia before you plan. When we checked in September 2026 it said to avoid non-essential travel, with stricter advisories for some regions. Advisories change, so read the live page on travel.gc.ca.

Nusuk Hajj is the Saudi platform for Hajj packages sold by authorised service providers in the countries it serves. Canada was on its list for the 2026 Hajj season. The list for 2027 had not been published when we checked on 23 September 2026. Nusuk says that registering does not mean you will be accepted for Hajj.
For Umrah, the Government of Canada page says any visa type can be used. Check the official Nusuk Umrah platform before you pay for travel.
Confirm the vaccine, visa, permit, and booking rules close to your departure date.
Ask a qualified teacher what you need to learn before you go.

scripts.title: Asking about qurbani
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm new and still learning about Eid al-Adha. Does qurbani apply to me this year, and is there a local or online option you'd trust?

scripts.title: Planning Hajj for later
scripts.body: I'm not ready for Hajj yet, but I want to know what I should be getting in order over the next few years. What should I learn first?

scripts.title: Checking a travel offer
scripts.body: Before I pay for this, could you help me check whether this Hajj or Umrah package goes through the official process, and whether anything about it looks off?

title: Yearly charity (zakat) for beginners
description: What zakat is, how nisab is measured, how to check a Canadian charity, and when to get a qualified review of your own numbers.
intro: Zakat is an obligation for Muslims whose wealth meets certain conditions. This page covers the vocabulary and the decision points. It is not a calculator, and it is not a ruling on your finances.
summary: Zakat is not the same thing as charity in general. Sadaqah is the voluntary kind.
The terms you will hear are nisab, hawl, and 2.5 percent.
Nisab is measured in grams of gold or silver, so its dollar value changes. Charities use slightly different figures.
Different assets get treated differently, so a personal case needs reviewing.
Quran 9:60 names eight categories of people who can receive zakat.
focusNow: Learn the basic terms: zakat, sadaqah, nisab, hawl, and who can receive it.
Notice whether your savings or assets might sit above the threshold.
If you think zakat applies to you, ask someone qualified.
Give through a registered charity that explains its zakat policy in plain terms.
canWait: A calculator inside this app.
Detailed sums for a business, a pension, debts, crypto, inheritance, or investments.
Treating one calculator online as the final word.
Arguing edge cases before you have the basics.

sections.heading: What zakat is
sections.body: Zakat is obligatory giving once a Muslim meets the conditions for it. It purifies wealth and goes to people who qualify to receive it. Sadaqah is different: voluntary charity, any amount, any time.

sections.heading: Who usually pays
sections.body: At a beginner level, zakat may apply if you own zakatable wealth above the nisab threshold for a lunar year. The details get complicated quickly, so do not panic if you cannot tell. Ask a qualified scholar or a zakat institution you trust.

sections.heading: If you are new to Islam
items: You owe no zakat for the years before you became Muslim.

A Shafi'i answer from SeekersGuidance (Shaykh Irshaad Sedick, 2022) says a new Muslim's first zakat is not due until a full lunar year has passed from the day they became Muslim. Other schools may count differently, so ask a teacher.
Write your Shahada date down, in the Hijri calendar as well if you can. Check your savings against the nisab on that date, and again one lunar year later.
Your zakat date is your own. If it falls before Ramadan, you do not have to wait for Ramadan to pay.

National Zakat Foundation Canada says most scholars allow paying zakat early, for example a set amount each month, as long as you already own the nisab and the full amount is paid by your zakat date. You then subtract what you have already paid when you work out the total. NZF describes a limit of two years ahead as a precaution some scholars add.

sections.heading: Nisab, hawl, and 2.5 percent
items: Nisab is the minimum wealth at which zakat becomes due. It is measured by weight: Islamic Relief Canada gives it as 87.48 grams of gold or 612.36 grams of silver.

Other Canadian charities use slightly different figures. National Zakat Foundation Canada uses 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver, and Muslim Welfare Canada's calculator uses 88 grams of gold or 613 grams of silver.
Some charities use the silver figure by default, which is lower, so more people pay and more people receive. Others use gold. Which one applies to you is a question for a scholar.
The dollar value moves with gold and silver prices, so this page does not give one. Use a current figure from the charity or scholar you follow.
Hawl is one lunar year, about 354 days, with your wealth staying above nisab.
2.5 percent is the rate for cash and savings. Some charities give 2.577 percent if you count by the ordinary calendar year instead of the lunar year.

sections.heading: Assets that raise questions
sections.body: Cash savings, gold, silver, business stock, investments, money owed to you, debts, and Canadian accounts such as an RRSP, TFSA or RESP each raise their own questions. National Zakat Foundation Canada, for example, says to count RRSP or TFSA money you can access at its value on your zakat date, and that you may subtract the tax withheld on an RRSP withdrawal. Muslim Welfare Canada's calculator only subtracts the coming year's payments on long-term debts. Scholars do not all agree, so use these as examples of the questions to ask, not as your answer.

sections.heading: Gold and silver jewellery
sections.body: Gold and silver jewellery is one of the clearest differences. National Zakat Foundation Canada's research page (Sheikh Nabil Khan, 2022) says the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools do not require zakat on women's jewellery that is worn, while the official Hanafi view is that zakat is due on all gold and silver, worn or not. NZF encourages paying as the cautious choice. Its page also explains how to count items that mix gold or silver with other metals. Ask which view your teacher follows.

sections.heading: The eight categories of recipients
sections.body: Quran 9:60 names eight categories of people who may receive zakat. Applying those categories takes knowledge of local need, organization policy, and scholarly interpretation, so work through a trusted zakat organization or ask someone qualified. Most scholars say zakat goes to Muslims. If your family is not Muslim and is struggling, help them from your other money or through voluntary charity (sadaqah), which is allowed and encouraged. The FAQ on zakat and non-Muslim family explains the differences.

sections.heading: If you are the one who needs help
sections.body: If your wealth is below nisab, zakat is not due from you, and if you are struggling you may be able to receive it. Some charities count new Muslims among those zakat can support. Penny Appeal Canada's policy, for example, reads the category of those whose hearts are to be reconciled as including new converts. Ask your masjid or a zakat charity. Needing help is nothing to be ashamed of.

sections.heading: Canadian registered charities
sections.body: These Canadian charities collect zakat and publish how they handle it. They are listed in alphabetical order with the registration number as each one shows it on its own site. This is not an endorsement, and other good options exist, including your local masjid.
items: Islamic Relief Canada: Registered Charity No. 821896875RR0001.
Muslim Welfare Canada: CRA Charity No. 89733-1732-RR0001.
National Zakat Foundation Canada: Registered Charity No. 839912599RR0001.
Penny Appeal Canada: CRA no. 827502741 RR0001.

sections.heading: Choosing where to give
items: Check the charity on the Canada Revenue Agency's list of charities before you give.
Look for a clear zakat policy, or a scholar who reviews their decisions.
Check that they explain who qualifies to receive it and what share goes to running costs.
Give to the charity itself, not to a person collecting for it, and do not give under pressure. Registered charities do not ask for gift cards.
Ask your local masjid who they trust to distribute zakat.
Keep your own records. Do not store personal financial details in this app.

If you give to a registered charity, ask for an official donation receipt. The Canada Revenue Agency gives federal and provincial tax credits for gifts to registered charities and other qualified donees, claimed on line 34900 of your return. Money handed straight to a person does not count. Whether a charity issues a receipt for zakat al-fitr or fidyah depends on the charity, so ask.

scripts.title: Asking a scholar
scripts.body: I'm new and trying to work out whether zakat applies to me. I have some savings, some debts, and a few assets. What should I bring so you can look at my case properly?

scripts.title: Asking a charity
scripts.body: Do you publish a zakat policy, and can you explain how you decide which campaigns or recipients are zakat-eligible?

scripts.title: When you are not sure
scripts.body: I don't want to guess with zakat. I'll learn the basics first, then ask someone qualified before I work out my own number.

title: Islamic calendar guide for beginners
description: Lunar months, why local dates differ, and how to ask your masjid what they follow.
intro: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so months start with the new moon, and announcements differ from one country, community, or sighting method to another. Keep it practical: learn the month names, confirm dates with the people near you, and do not take a graphic you saw online as the final word for your city.
summary: Islamic months follow the moon, so the dates move around the solar year.
Some communities go by local moon sighting, some follow a regional or global announcement, and some use a calculated calendar.
Confirm Ramadan, Eid, Ashura, and the Hajj days with a masjid you trust or an official community announcement.
When two communities announce different dates, stay calm and ask which one your masjid follows.
focusNow: Learn the months you will actually hear about: Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram, Rajab, and Sha'ban.
Ask your masjid how they announce the dates for Ramadan, Eid, and Ashura.
Pick one local source you trust so you are not drowning in conflicting posts.
Leave the detailed calendar debates for a qualified teacher.
canWait: Learning every moon-sighting method.
Arguing online about global against local sighting.
Calendar reminders or saved date tracking in this app.
Memorizing all the month names before you know what they are for.

sections.heading: Why the dates move
sections.body: The Islamic calendar counts lunar months rather than following the solar calendar behind most civil dates. A lunar year is shorter, so Ramadan, Eid, and the other Islamic dates drift earlier through the seasons year after year.

sections.heading: Why local dates differ
sections.body: One community may announce a month a day apart from another because they use a different sighting policy or a different official calendar. For a new Muslim the practical answer is simple: follow the masjid or Muslim organization you will actually pray and celebrate with.

sections.heading: How to confirm a date
items: Check your masjid's website, mailing list, WhatsApp group, or social feed.
Look for a clear announcement from a recognized local council or Muslim organization.
If you are going to Eid prayer, confirm the place and the time as well as the date.
If the announcements differ, just ask which calendar your masjid follows.

sections.heading: Months you will hear often
items: Ramadan is the month of fasting.
Shawwal opens with Eid al-Fitr.
Dhul Hijjah holds Hajj and Eid al-Adha.
Muharram is the first month of the Islamic year, and Ashura falls in it.
Rajab and Sha'ban come up when people start preparing for Ramadan.

sections.heading: A calm rule for beginners
sections.body: Use a calendar for planning and confirm worship dates locally. That keeps you in step with the people you pray with and saves you a panic when two posts online disagree.

scripts.title: Asking a masjid
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm new and trying to keep up with the Islamic calendar. How does this masjid announce Ramadan, Eid, Ashura, and the other important dates?

scripts.title: When the dates differ
scripts.body: I've seen a couple of different dates online. Which announcement should I go by if I'm planning to pray with your community?

scripts.title: For work or school
scripts.body: The exact date of this observance gets confirmed close to the day, because it follows the Islamic lunar calendar. I'll let you know as soon as my community announces it.

title: The first month and its fast (Muharram and Ashura)
description: What Muharram and Ashura are, where voluntary fasting fits, and what to ask locally.
intro: Muharram is the first month of the Islamic year and one of the sacred months. Ashura is its tenth day. Keep this season simple to begin with: learn what it means, confirm the local date, and fast if you are able and have been guided properly.
summary: Muharram is one of the four sacred months named in hadith.
Ashura is the tenth day of Muharram.
Voluntary fasting in Muharram, and on Ashura in particular, is established in authentic hadith.
If fasting is hard on you, unsafe, or unclear in your situation, ask someone qualified and pick another good deed.
focusNow: Ask your masjid when they are observing Ashura.
If you can fast safely, ask whether your community fasts one day or two.
Spend the day on prayer, dhikr, charity, and reflection, without inventing rituals for it.
Leave the dramatic claims online alone unless a reliable source teaches them.
canWait: Historical debates you are not yet equipped to judge.
Taking every viral Ashura checklist as established Sunnah.
Guilt over a voluntary fast you could not keep because of health, work, medication, or plain confusion.
Calendar reminders and saved fast tracking.

sections.heading: What Muharram is
sections.body: Muharram is the first month of the Islamic lunar year and one of the sacred months. You do not need a program for it. Extra worship, repentance, charity, and kindness are a fine place to start.

sections.heading: What Ashura is
sections.body: Ashura is the tenth day of Muharram. Authentic hadith mention fasting that day and tie it to gratitude to Allah. Ask your masjid which date they are using, since local announcements differ.

sections.heading: Fasting without pressure
items: Fasting Ashura is voluntary. It is not the Ramadan fast.
If you are able to fast, ask a local teacher whether to fast Ashura by itself or alongside another day.
If fasting could harm you, talk to a clinician and to a qualified religious teacher.
If you cannot fast, make dhikr, give charity, read Quran, or do something quietly useful for someone.

sections.heading: Weakly sourced practices
sections.body: Do not take every ritual, promise, or dramatic post about Ashura as established. If a practice does not trace back to reliable Quran, hadith, or qualified teaching, keep it as your own good deed or leave it until you can ask.

sections.heading: If the day feels heavy
sections.body: Some communities mark painful history around Muharram. You can listen respectfully and stay out of the arguments. Ask a reliable teacher what is most useful for a beginner to learn first.

scripts.title: Asking about Ashura
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm new and I've heard about Ashura. What date is the community observing, and what should a beginner focus on?

scripts.title: When health is a factor
scripts.body: I'd like to fast voluntarily, but I have a health and medication concern. Who can help me ask the medical side and the religious side properly?

scripts.title: When a post seems off
scripts.body: I saw a list of special Ashura practices online. Could you help me tell which parts are authentic and which I shouldn't treat as established?

title: The Prophet's birth month (Rabi al-Awwal)
description: Let Rabi al-Awwal remind you to learn the Prophet's life and character, without getting pulled into arguments.
intro: Rabi al-Awwal is when Muslims tend to talk more about the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Keep it beginner-sized: learn his mercy, his character, what he was sent with, and the everyday Sunnah, from teachers you can rely on, and stay out of the fights.
summary: Muslims love the Prophet and study his life because he is the Messenger of Allah and the example believers follow.
Seerah means the life story of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.
Rabi al-Awwal is a good month to start a reliable seerah class or book.
Stay out of online arguments about commemorations until you have a teacher.
focusNow: Read a short, reliable introduction to the Prophet's life.
Pick one daily Sunnah of character: honest speech, mercy, cleanliness, or kindness at home.
Ask a teacher for a beginner seerah book or class.
If someone starts arguing about Rabi al-Awwal practices, step back and ask a qualified scholar instead.
canWait: Detailed timelines with every battle and date.
Online debates about Mawlid or commemorations.
Trying to copy every Sunnah at once.
Answering hostile claims before you know the basics yourself.

sections.heading: What to learn first
items: Who the Prophet was and why Muslims love him.
His message of worshipping Allah alone.
His mercy, patience, truthfulness, and concern for people.
How hadith and Sunnah connect to ordinary Muslim life.

sections.heading: A beginner path
sections.body: Start with a short overview, then move to a structured class or book from a teacher you can rely on. You do not need to memorize dates. The message, the character, and the broad stages of Makkah and Madinah matter more at the start.

sections.heading: If the debates come up
sections.body: Muslims differ over certain commemorations and gatherings. You do not have to take a side yet. You can say that you are focusing on learning the Prophet's life and that you ask qualified teachers about the details of practice.

sections.heading: One practical Sunnah this month
items: Speak truthfully and gently.
Keep one promise you made.
Send blessings on the Prophet, using a wording you have actually been taught.
Show mercy to someone who is new, tired, or misunderstood.

scripts.title: Asking for a seerah book
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm new and I want to learn the Prophet's life in a calm, reliable way. Is there a beginner book, class, or teacher you'd recommend?

scripts.title: Stepping out of a debate
scripts.body: I'm still on the basics, so I'd rather not argue about this. I'm working on learning the Prophet's life and character from teachers I can rely on.

scripts.title: A goal for yourself
scripts.body: This month I want to work on one Sunnah of character: kinder speech, honesty, mercy, or patience.

title: The two months before Ramadan (Rajab and Sha'ban)
description: Get ready for Ramadan carefully, and keep a source check on Rajab and Sha'ban practices.
intro: Rajab and Sha'ban come just before Ramadan, and they bring a flood of online reminders with them. This page helps you prepare without treating weakly sourced claims as established worship.
summary: Rajab is one of the sacred months. Be careful with the special claims made about it that carry no source.
For Sha'ban there are authentic reports of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, fasting more often.
Preparing can be simple: fix your sleep, learn the basics of fasting, ask your awkward questions early, and build up worship gradually.
Before you take on a special night, prayer, or promise you only saw online, ask a qualified teacher.
focusNow: Go over the Ramadan basics before the month starts.
Ask early about medication, illness, travel, menstruation, missed fasts, and fidyah.
Practice one small habit: an earlier bedtime, listening to Quran, a small charity, or a short dua.
Keep the Rajab and Sha'ban claims source-checked, and keep your head.
canWait: Verifying every viral calendar post yourself.
Special prayers or fasts with no reliable source.
Filling your schedule up before Ramadan even begins.
Judging other Muslims while you are still learning.

sections.heading: Rajab, without overclaiming
sections.body: Rajab is named among the sacred months in hadith. For a beginner that is reason enough to treat it seriously and do good in it. Do not present a particular Rajab prayer, fast, or promise as established unless a qualified teacher gives you a reliable source for it.

sections.heading: Sha'ban, and gentle preparation
sections.body: Authentic hadith mention the Prophet fasting often in Sha'ban. If you are able and already used to fasting, ask a teacher how voluntary fasts might fit your health and your schedule. If you are not there yet, prepare in other ways.

sections.heading: Practical preparation
items: Find out how your masjid announces Ramadan.
Go over the basics of suhoor, iftar, Taraweeh, and Eid.
Ask the awkward fasting questions before Ramadan starts.
Set a Quran, dhikr, or charity goal you can actually hit.

sections.heading: Where to draw the source line
sections.body: If a post promises a specific reward for a specific Rajab or Sha'ban act and gives no reliable source, do not pass it on as Islamic guidance. You can still do the good deed without the claim attached to it.

scripts.title: Asking before Ramadan
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. Ramadan is coming and I'm new to this. Could I ask now about fasting, medication, travel, menstruation, missed fasts, or anything personal that might affect me?

scripts.title: Checking a claim
scripts.body: I saw a special Rajab or Sha'ban practice online. Is it from a reliable source, or should I treat it as general personal worship only?

scripts.title: A small goal
scripts.body: Before Ramadan I'm picking one habit I can keep: sleeping earlier, drinking more water at suhoor, reading a short portion of Quran, or giving a small charity.

title: Charity and service all year
description: How sadaqah, service, and looking after people fit your life outside Ramadan and zakat season.
intro: Charity belongs to the whole year, and it covers more than money. Islam encourages giving, service, mercy, and small everyday good deeds in every month. This page helps a beginner pick something simple without straining their finances.
summary: Zakat is obligatory once its conditions apply. Sadaqah is voluntary.
Service can be your time, your skills, food, a listening ear, or looking after people around you.
Small steady good deeds beat a burst you cannot keep up.
Your own zakat, debts, taxes, and fundraising questions need a qualified financial and religious review.
focusNow: Pick one act of service each month that you can keep up.
Give only what you can afford. Do not cut into your rent, your food, or the people who depend on you.
Give to organizations that are open about their finances, or to local needs you can check yourself.
Ask your masjid where the help is needed rather than guessing.
canWait: Complicated zakat sums without a qualified review.
Feeling obliged to every fundraiser that reaches you.
Announcing your donations publicly.
Storing donation records or personal finances in this app.

sections.heading: Charity beyond money
sections.body: Sadaqah can be money, and it can also be service and ordinary decency. The aim for a beginner is not to give past your capacity. Start with something sincere that you can keep doing.

sections.heading: Simple ways to serve
items: Bring food to a community iftar or a class when that fits.
Volunteer for setup, cleanup, rides, or greeting people at the door.
Check on a convert or an elder who is on their own, with their permission and without making a show of it.
Share something reliable instead of a quote graphic with no source.
Make dua for someone privately, then follow it with practical help if you can.

sections.heading: Choosing where to give
items: Look for a clear organization name, a clear purpose, and a donation policy.
Prefer official charity pages or masjid campaigns you can check locally.
If the donation is zakat, ask how they handle zakat funds specifically.
Walk away from pressure, shame, vague emergency claims, and anonymous payment links.

sections.heading: When money is tight
sections.body: Not being able to give money does not make you less sincere. Offer time, a kind word, practical help, or one small thing you do consistently. If you are the one struggling, ask your masjid or a trusted support service what is available.

sections.heading: Where this page stops
sections.body: This page does not calculate zakat, assess your debts, or advise on tax, investments, or fundraising law. Take personal financial cases to qualified scholars, zakat advisors, financial professionals, or the relevant official agency.

scripts.title: Asking where to help
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm new and I'd like to help with something simple. Is there a small volunteer job or a community need I could take on?

scripts.title: Checking a fundraiser
scripts.body: Before I donate, could you help me check whether this organization is identifiable and whether the campaign says where the money goes?

scripts.title: When the budget is tight
scripts.body: I want to give, but money is tight right now. I'm going to pick something I can do with my time instead, and keep my own essentials covered.
